C0001  extended reality  [defined; from fact 1/S1/F0]
  Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

C0002  virtual reality  [defined; from fact 4/S0/F2]
  Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

C0003  augmented reality  [defined; from fact 1/S2/F1]
  Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.

C0004  mixed reality  [defined; from fact 1/S2/F3]
  Mixed reality, in a broad sense, is the entire space between the real environment extreme and the virtual environment extreme of the reality-virtuality continuum, containing different degrees of augmentation of the real environment with virtual content and of the virtual environment with real content.

C0005  headset  [not defined; from fact 1/S0/F1]
  To different people, hearing extended reality (XR), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), or mixed reality (MR) may lead them to associate one or more of these terms with magical movie scenes such as those in Avatar, interactive video games, 3D or 4D movie-theater documentaries about extinct animals, a user wearing a headset that blocks vision and transports the user to a virtual world, which is the most common perception of VR, games such as Pokémon Go in which the real world is visible on a device screen and virtual objects that do not exist in the real world can also be seen on that screen, or visualizations of internal body structures such as a skeleton or veins.

C0006  virtual world  [not defined; from fact 1/S0/F1]
  To different people, hearing extended reality (XR), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), or mixed reality (MR) may lead them to associate one or more of these terms with magical movie scenes such as those in Avatar, interactive video games, 3D or 4D movie-theater documentaries about extinct animals, a user wearing a headset that blocks vision and transports the user to a virtual world, which is the most common perception of VR, games such as Pokémon Go in which the real world is visible on a device screen and virtual objects that do not exist in the real world can also be seen on that screen, or visualizations of internal body structures such as a skeleton or veins.

C0008  immersive technology  [defined; from fact 1/S1/F0]
  Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

C0009  immersive experience  [defined; from fact 1/S1/F2]
  An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

C0010  reality-virtuality continuum  [defined; from fact 1/S2/F0]
  The reality-virtuality continuum is a scale whose extremes are a completely real environment with nothing virtual and a completely virtual environment with nothing real.

C0011  augmented virtuality  [defined; from fact 1/S2/F2]
  Augmented virtuality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state, opposite augmented reality, in which the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content.

C0012  market size  [not defined; from fact 1/S3/F1]
  A market study reports that the extended reality market size was about 20.5 billion US dollars in 2021 and is expected to be about 860 billion US dollars by 2030, an exponential increase.

C0013  hardware  [not defined; from fact 1/S3/F2]

C0014  software  [not defined; from fact 1/S3/F2]
  The hardware market in the extended reality market is about 60 percent of the market size, and the software market is about 40 percent.

C0015  metaverse  [defined; from fact 1/S3/F4]

C0016  three-dimensional environment  [not defined; from fact 1/S3/F6]

C0043  immersive simulation  [not defined; from fact 2/S0/F3]

C0045  heritage tourism  [defined; from fact 2/S0/F7]

C0056  virtual reality system  [defined; from fact 4/S1/F0]
  A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

C0883  linear acceleration  [not defined; from fact 17/S0/F1]

C0884  magnetic field strength  [not defined; from fact 17/S0/F1]

C0885  drift error  [not defined; from fact 17/S0/F2]
  Inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor tracking relies mainly on gyroscope readings of angular velocity, while the accelerometer and magnetometer do not directly contribute to the tracking estimation but can be used to detect drift errors and take corrective measures.

C0886  measured angular velocity  [not defined; from fact 17/S1/F0]
  In the calibration of inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors, a gyroscope provides angular velocity, and the measured angular velocity (omega_g) can differ from the actual angular velocity (omega_a) because the devices and measurement technique are imperfect, so the measurement error is omega_g minus omega_a.

C0887  actual angular velocity  [not defined; from fact 17/S1/F0]

C0888  measurement error  [defined; from fact 17/S1/F0]
  In the calibration of inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors, a gyroscope provides angular velocity, and the measured angular velocity (omega_g) can differ from the actual angular velocity (omega_a) because the devices and measurement technique are imperfect, so the measurement error is omega_g minus omega_a.

C0889  calibration model  [not defined; from fact 17/S1/F2]
  One simple calibration model assumes a linear relationship between measured angular velocity (omega_g) and actual angular velocity (omega_a), for example omega_g = a + b omega_a, where the ideal condition omega_g = omega_a corresponds to a = 0 and b = 1, but this ideal condition never happens in practice and the linear relationship is not the only possible relationship.

C0890  linear relationship  [not defined; from fact 17/S1/F2]
  One simple calibration model assumes a linear relationship between measured angular velocity (omega_g) and actual angular velocity (omega_a), for example omega_g = a + b omega_a, where the ideal condition omega_g = omega_a corresponds to a = 0 and b = 1, but this ideal condition never happens in practice and the linear relationship is not the only possible relationship.

C0891  paired samples  [defined; from fact 17/S1/F3]
  The presented calibration uses many, sometimes thousands, paired samples from two sensors: a cheap, inaccurate inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor that produces the measured values (omega_g), and an expensive, highly accurate benchmark sensor that produces the actual values (omega_a), although the benchmark is very close rather than exact or ideal.

C0892  benchmark sensor  [not defined; from fact 17/S1/F3]
  The presented calibration uses many, sometimes thousands, paired samples from two sensors: a cheap, inaccurate inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor that produces the measured values (omega_g), and an expensive, highly accurate benchmark sensor that produces the actual values (omega_a), although the benchmark is very close rather than exact or ideal.

C0893  linear least squares regression  [defined; from fact 17/S1/F4]
  A simple calibration method compares the paired samples by computing, for n pairs, the sum of the squared differences between the expression C1 + C2 omega_g and the actual values omega_a, and it finds the constants C1 and C2 that minimize this sum; this classical optimization is linear least squares regression, one of many techniques that is used here for simplicity.

C0894  calibrated value  [defined; from fact 17/S1/F5]
  After the constants C1 and C2 are determined, calibration mathematically transforms the cheap sensor reading into a calibrated value omega_cal, defined as omega_cal = C1 + C2 omega_g, mapping the inexpensive measured angular velocity omega_g to the closest possible match with the actual value rather than by using an actually expensive or highly accurate sensor.

C0896  initial alignment  [defined; from fact 17/S2/F0]

C0897  tracking system  [not defined; from fact 17/S2/F1]

C0898  reflector  [not defined; from fact 17/S2/F2]

C0900  current sensor orientation  [defined; from fact 17/S2/F3]

C0901  calibrated angular velocity sample  [defined; from fact 17/S2/F3]

C0902  sampling interval  [not defined; from fact 17/S2/F3]

C0904  angular velocity sample  [not defined; from fact 17/S2/F4]
  A calibrated angular velocity sample W_cal_i is the angular velocity sample from a gyroscopic sensor at instant i, and it indicates a change in orientation equal to W_cal_i multiplied by the sampling interval delta_t.

C0905  gyroscopic sensor  [not defined; from fact 17/S2/F4]
  A calibrated angular velocity sample W_cal_i is the angular velocity sample from a gyroscopic sensor at instant i, and it indicates a change in orientation equal to W_cal_i multiplied by the sampling interval delta_t.

C0906  drift  [not defined; from fact 17/S3/F0]
  Drift correction is usually done with the help of extra sensors and, in general, requires at least two sensors whose values are blended to estimate and correct drift.

C0907  drift-corrected orientation  [defined; from fact 17/S3/F2]
  A classic approach to drift correction combines the two individually computed orientations at the same time instant using the expression theta_dk = alpha theta_gk + (1 - alpha) theta_ck, where theta_gk is the orientation obtained by integrating gyroscope values at the kth instant, theta_ck is the orientation obtained with a camera at the kth instant, theta_dk is the drift-corrected orientation, and alpha is the gain parameter, a normalized value between 0 and 1.

C0908  gain parameter  [defined; from fact 17/S3/F2]
  A classic approach to drift correction combines the two individually computed orientations at the same time instant using the expression theta_dk = alpha theta_gk + (1 - alpha) theta_ck, where theta_gk is the orientation obtained by integrating gyroscope values at the kth instant, theta_ck is the orientation obtained with a camera at the kth instant, theta_dk is the drift-corrected orientation, and alpha is the gain parameter, a normalized value between 0 and 1.

C0913  vision-based tracking  [not defined; from fact 18/S0/F0]

C1639  Stevens' power law  [defined; from fact 30/S1/F2]
  Stevens' power law is a result from psychophysics that characterizes the relationship between the magnitude of a physical stimulus and its perceived magnitude by the equation P = C M^x, where M is the magnitude or intensity of the original stimulus, P is the perceived magnitude, x is the exponent that relates actual magnitude to perceived magnitude, and C is a constant that depends on units.

C1640  perceived magnitude  [not defined; from fact 30/S1/F2]

C1641  exponent  [not defined; from fact 30/S1/F2]

C1642  just noticeable difference  [defined; from fact 30/S1/F3]
  The just noticeable difference (JND) is a result from psychophysics that specifies the amount of change in a stimulus that is required for subjects to perceive it as changed in at least 50 percent of trials.

C1643  Weber's law  [defined; from fact 30/S1/F4]
  Weber's law captures the just noticeable difference (JND), the change in magnitude that is noticeable, by representing it as delta M divided by M equals C, where M is the magnitude or intensity of the stimulus, delta M is the just noticeable difference, and C is a constant; equivalently, delta M equals M times C.

C1644  auditory perception  [not defined; from fact 30/S1/F5]
  Weber's law and Stevens' power law are laws from psychophysics that also apply to psychoacoustics, or auditory perception, when physical stimuli are replaced by acoustic stimuli.

C1652  spherical coordinate system  [defined; from fact 30/S3/F2]

C1653  azimuth  [defined; from fact 30/S3/F3]
  The spherical coordinate system used to represent a sound source location has three parameters: azimuth, the angle in the horizontal plane between the forward direction and the projection of the sound source direction, ranging from -180 degrees to 180 degrees; elevation, the angle between the actual source direction and the horizontal plane, ranging from -90 degrees to 90 degrees; and radius, the distance from the listener's head origin to the source.

C1661  acoustic shadow  [defined; from fact 30/S4/F2]

C1662  interaural time difference  [defined; from fact 30/S4/F3]
  Interaural time difference is a binaural sound localization cue from different sound arrival times at the ears; in an average human head, the ears are 21.5 centimeters apart, sound travels that distance in about 0.6 milliseconds, and this small time difference can be used to locate the source.

C1783  iterative design  [not defined; from fact 32/S5/F0]

C1784  development cost  [not defined; from fact 32/S5/F1]

  Target occlusion can also be an important factor in selection performance: if a target is partly occluded by other surrounding objects, locating and selecting it is challenging and specialized techniques may be required, while fully occluded objects may also be selected, but the user must first be made aware of their presence, and specialized selection of fully occluded objects is a special case, with the majority of cases involving partially occluded or partially visible objects.

C2048  selection with the hand  [not defined; from fact 39/S1/F3]
  Object selection techniques in a virtual world include selection with the hand, pointing-based selection, image plane selection, volume-based selection, and bimanual selection.

C2049  pointing-based selection  [defined; from fact 39/S3/F0]
  Pointing-based selection is a selection technique in which the user operates a controller to extend a ray into the distance in the virtual world, sees the ray, and can select the first object intersected by the ray through a user-controlled trigger on the controller.

C2050  image plane selection  [defined; from fact 39/S4/F0]

C2053  hand selection technique  [defined; from fact 39/S2/F0]

C2054  grab  [not defined; from fact 39/S2/F0]

C2059  one-to-one mapping  [not defined; from fact 39/S2/F2]
  The virtual hand technique is the simplest and most intuitive hand selection technique, in which a visible virtual hand acts as an avatar of the user's physical hand and is tied to it through a one-to-one mapping of the physical hand's motion and orientation, typically implemented with three-dimensional (3D) tracked controllers, allowing natural hand movements.

C2060  three-dimensional tracked controller  [not defined; from fact 39/S2/F2]
  The virtual hand technique is the simplest and most intuitive hand selection technique, in which a visible virtual hand acts as an avatar of the user's physical hand and is tied to it through a one-to-one mapping of the physical hand's motion and orientation, typically implemented with three-dimensional (3D) tracked controllers, allowing natural hand movements.

C2061  virtual arm length  [defined; from fact 39/S2/F4]
  The go-go technique is a virtual hand selection technique for distant objects that allows the user to interactively change the virtual arm length, the length of the virtual hand, uses one-to-one mapping when the target is close, and, as distance increases, maps smaller physical hand movements to larger and faster virtual hand movements, possibly exponentially, so that distant objects can be reached quickly.

C2062  hand velocity  [not defined; from fact 39/S2/F6]
  The prism technique is an improvement of the go-go technique that applies scaled-down motion to the virtual hand when the user's physical hand moves below a specified speed, and if the hand velocity is slower than a specified minimum velocity, the virtual hand remains still.

C2063  proximity sphere  [defined; from fact 39/S2/F10]
  Intent-driven selection techniques typically use proximity spheres that encompass multiple objects at a larger distance and progressively reduce in size, depending on hand or finger postures, as the user moves closer to the intended object, refining the selection to a specific object.

C2064  travel technique  [not defined; from fact 39/S2/F11]
  In hand selection techniques, go-go and prism are travel techniques, intent-driven selection is a grabbing technique, and intent-driven selection may be combined with a go-go or prism travel technique.

C2065  grabbing technique  [not defined; from fact 39/S2/F11]
  In hand selection techniques, go-go and prism are travel techniques, intent-driven selection is a grabbing technique, and intent-driven selection may be combined with a go-go or prism travel technique.

C2072  ray casting  [defined; from fact 39/S3/F4]

C2073  bend cast  [defined; from fact 39/S3/F6]
  Bend cast is an improvement over basic ray casting in which the system bends the ray toward the closest selectable object, detected by calculating the point-line distance from each selectable object, so the user need not point precisely, and a circular arc can provide visual feedback for the bending.

C2074  selectable object  [not defined; from fact 39/S3/F6]

C2076  depth ray  [defined; from fact 39/S3/F8]

C2077  depth marker  [not defined; from fact 39/S3/F8]

C2163  environment design  [defined; from fact 40/S5/F3]

C2164  wayfinding mental model  [defined; from fact 40/S5/F4]
  The spatial knowledge in a wayfinding mental model consists of landmark knowledge of the surroundings and other places, procedural knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path, and topological or map-like knowledge of the overall environment, together forming the essential knowledge base of the mental model.

C2169  wayfinding support  [defined; from fact 40/S5/F6]
  For a good immersive user experience in a complex virtual environment with many objects and different ways to reach targets, wayfinding support is essential; locomotion or travel support alone is not sufficient, and regardless of how many or how sophisticated the travel techniques are, without suitable wayfinding support the user cannot use them efficiently or effectively.

C2170  locomotion or travel support  [not defined; from fact 40/S5/F6]
  For a good immersive user experience in a complex virtual environment with many objects and different ways to reach targets, wayfinding support is essential; locomotion or travel support alone is not sufficient, and regardless of how many or how sophisticated the travel techniques are, without suitable wayfinding support the user cannot use them efficiently or effectively.

C2171  landmark support  [defined; from fact 40/S5/F7]
  Landmark support for wayfinding uses obvious distinct non-mobile objects positioned in a given place, and a good landmark should be clearly visible from several different locations or viewpoints.

C2172  landmark  [defined; from fact 40/S5/F7]
  Landmark support for wayfinding uses obvious distinct non-mobile objects positioned in a given place, and a good landmark should be clearly visible from several different locations or viewpoints.

C2173  map support  [defined; from fact 40/S5/F8]
  Map support for wayfinding can provide maps of the space or place, such as a copy of the virtual world map, where the term world means the virtual world rather than the real world, or a world in miniature display that can show the entire virtual world with objects at different points, the current position of the user, and different routes to different points.

C2174  world in miniature display  [defined; from fact 40/S5/F8]

C2175  path following support  [defined; from fact 40/S5/F9]
  Path following support for wayfinding can denote multiple paths through a single space by colors, so the user knows that there are different paths to reach a destination.

C2176  breadcrumb support  [defined; from fact 40/S5/F10]
  Breadcrumb support for wayfinding leaves a trail of markers along the path followed by predecessors, so users can recognize that a path has already been explored, avoid getting lost, and choose another path or destination to save time.

C2241  virtual vehicle travel technique  [defined; from fact 41/S6/F5]
  The virtual vehicle travel technique gives the user a seated viewpoint inside the vehicle when it is selected, changes the surrounding scenes as the vehicle moves to create the feeling of motion, and lets the user operate the vehicle through ray casting interactions to provide a direction of movement and select a destination, to which the vehicle moves.

C2251  point of interest  [defined; from fact 53/S1/F0]
  The Satra campus is modeled as a graph in which the points of interest (POI) are the nodes, the graph has at least 25 nodes, and the edges connecting pairs of nodes are weighted by the Euclidean distance between the corresponding points of interest.

C2252  point-of-interest awareness  [not defined; from fact 41/S7/F3]
  In the virtual tour system, point-of-interest awareness is supported by directional arrows that indicate which way to move and guide users toward points of interest, and by information icons that, when selected, provide further details about the place, mostly as textual information, so users do not overlook important elements in the environment.

C2253  directional arrow  [defined; from fact 41/S7/F3]
  In the virtual tour system, point-of-interest awareness is supported by directional arrows that indicate which way to move and guide users toward points of interest, and by information icons that, when selected, provide further details about the place, mostly as textual information, so users do not overlook important elements in the environment.

C2254  controlled navigation technique  [defined; from fact 41/S8/F0]
  The system design implemented a controlled navigation technique to minimize cybersickness, in which users navigate or teleport using a joystick, so that controlled movement does not support abrupt movements that can cause discomfort and reduces the chances of discomfort.

C2255  vehicular movement  [not defined; from fact 41/S8/F1]

C2256  speed of change of viewpoint  [not defined; from fact 41/S8/F1]
  In vehicular movement, the speed of change of viewpoint may cause cybersickness if it is not chosen carefully.

C2269  cost overrun  [not defined; from fact 42/S1/F2]

C2277  low-fidelity prototype  [defined; from fact 42/S4/F0]

C2278  low-fidelity prototyping  [defined; from fact 42/S4/F1]

C2280  interface sketch  [defined; from fact 42/S4/F3]
  An interface sketch is a simple drawing that can be made on paper and depicts the major components of an interface, including the screen elements the user sees, buttons, selection options, their appearance, and their layout, so that an interface idea can be expressed to others or users for comments and feedback and its appearance can be envisioned.

C2281  storyboard  [defined; from fact 42/S4/F5]
  To represent interaction, a low-fidelity prototype needs a series of interface sketches rather than a single sketch, a practice often called storyboarding; a single sketch gives a horizontal prototype, whereas a series of sketches can give a vertical prototype depicting interaction.

C2282  keyframe  [defined; from fact 42/S4/F6]
  In a storyboard, each sketch is a keyframe, which is a snapshot of the interaction at a particular point in time; the keyframes visualize the interaction for a specific task and its corresponding scenes, and the storyboard captures the sequence of user actions and the screen appearances the user sees from the beginning of the task to its end.

C2336  Nielsen's ten heuristics  [defined; from fact 43/S3/F2]
  Nielsen's 10 heuristics is a general set of heuristics proposed in 1994 that is primarily related to graphical user interfaces (GUIs) but equally applicable to most interactive systems.

C2337  visibility of system status  [defined; from fact 43/S3/F3]
  Nielsen's 10 heuristics consist of: 1) visibility of system status, in which the status of the system should be visible to the user; 2) match between system and the real world, in which what the user does on the system should closely match the user's real-world experience; 3) user control and freedom, concerning whether the user is given freedom and what kind of controls are provided; 4) consistency and standards, in which elements and layout should be consistent across different screens and standards should be followed; 5) error prevention, in which the design should help the user prevent errors; 6) recognition rather than recall, in which the user should not have to remember what to do but should be able to recognize from elements what to do because recollection is more difficult than recognition; 7) flexibility and efficiency of use; 8) aesthetic and minimalist design, in which the design should have a minimum number of elements and should be aesthetically pleasing; 9) help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors; and 10) help and documentation, in which the system should provide help and documentation support.

  Nielsen's 10 heuristics consist of: 1) visibility of system status, in which the status of the system should be visible to the user; 2) match between system and the real world, in which what the user does on the system should closely match the user's real-world experience; 3) user control and freedom, concerning whether the user is given freedom and what kind of controls are provided; 4) consistency and standards, in which elements and layout should be consistent across different screens and standards should be followed; 5) error prevention, in which the design should help the user prevent errors; 6) recognition rather than recall, in which the user should not have to remember what to do but should be able to recognize from elements what to do because recollection is more difficult than recognition; 7) flexibility and efficiency of use; 8) aesthetic and minimalist design, in which the design should have a minimum number of elements and should be aesthetically pleasing; 9) help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors; and 10) help and documentation, in which the system should provide help and documentation support.

  Nielsen's 10 heuristics consist of: 1) visibility of system status, in which the status of the system should be visible to the user; 2) match between system and the real world, in which what the user does on the system should closely match the user's real-world experience; 3) user control and freedom, concerning whether the user is given freedom and what kind of controls are provided; 4) consistency and standards, in which elements and layout should be consistent across different screens and standards should be followed; 5) error prevention, in which the design should help the user prevent errors; 6) recognition rather than recall, in which the user should not have to remember what to do but should be able to recognize from elements what to do because recollection is more difficult than recognition; 7) flexibility and efficiency of use; 8) aesthetic and minimalist design, in which the design should have a minimum number of elements and should be aesthetically pleasing; 9) help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors; and 10) help and documentation, in which the system should provide help and documentation support.

C2346  user evaluation  [defined; from fact 44/S0/F0]

C2349  questionnaire  [defined; from fact 44/S0/F3]
  In user evaluation, the items provided to users to rate are questions or statements, and these items are commonly called questionnaires although they need not contain questions.

C2350  post-task data collection  [not defined; from fact 44/S0/F5]
  In user evaluation, data can be collected after every task and at the end of the session, collecting data at both points is desirable if feasible, otherwise one of the two points must be chosen, and suitable questionnaires must be created for the point at which data are collected, so the questionnaires used after every task need not be the same as those used after the whole session.

C2351  after scenario questionnaire  [defined; from fact 44/S1/F0]
  The After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) is a post-task questionnaire consisting of three statements: 'I am satisfied with the ease of completing the tasks in this scenario'; 'I am satisfied with the amount of time it took to complete the tasks in this scenario'; and 'I am satisfied with the support information that is comprised of online help, messages, documentation when completing the tasks'.

C2363  five-point agreement scale  [defined; from fact 44/S2/F2]
  Each System Usability Scale (SUS) statement is rated by the user on a 5-point agreement scale, where 1 indicates strongly disagree and 5 indicates strongly agree.

C2364  System Usability Scale score  [defined; from fact 44/S2/F3]
  The System Usability Scale (SUS) score S is calculated from all 10 statement ratings r_i, with i from 1 to 10, as S = 2.5 × (Σ_{i∈{1,3,5,7,9}}(r_i − 1) + Σ_{i∈{2,4,6,8,10}}(5 − r_i)), where r_i is the user's rating for statement i.

C2365  statement rating  [defined; from fact 44/S2/F2]

C2366  expert evaluation technique  [not defined; from fact 44/S2/F5]
  Unlike expert evaluation techniques, which give designers more detailed reports from each evaluator, the System Usability Scale (SUS) gives a quick general indication from user ratings of whether usability problems exist but does not explain the reasons, so designers must identify the specific problems through further brainstorming or by examining the scores of individual statements.

C2367  design review  [not defined; from fact 44/S2/F4]
  The System Usability Scale (SUS) score is interpreted directly as a percentage, and a score of 70% or higher is typically considered desirable, indicating that the interface is usable or has only minimal problems, while a score below 70% may indicate usability problems that may require a design review.

C2615  slow-in-slow-out pattern  [defined; from fact 50/S2/F1]

C2616  slow-in-slow-out walking pattern  [not defined; from fact 50/S3/F0]

C2624  visual gain  [defined; from fact 50/S3/F5]

C2625  instantaneous step frequency  [not defined; from fact 50/S3/F5]
  The desired perceived scene-change speed, denoted v_visual or v_perceived, is computed by multiplying the visual gain g by the actual instantaneous walking speed v_actual, so v_visual = g × v_actual, where v_actual is the user's movement speed and is related to the instantaneous step frequency.

C2626  initial frequency  [defined; from fact 50/S3/F8]
  The instantaneous step frequency f(x) is computed from the Fourier-series expression f(x) = (4/π) × 1.8 × Σ_{k=0}^{d/2−1} [1/(2k+1) × sin((2k+1)ωx)], where ω = 2πf0, f0 is the initial frequency and equals 1/(2d), and d is the distance between the source and destination.

C2641  virtual reality navigation experience  [not defined; from fact 51/S0/F2]
  The approach to optimizing virtual reality (VR) navigation experience that uses the natural walking model addresses cyber sickness by controlling the duration of exposure in the virtual world.

C2642  virtual reality environment  [not defined; from fact 51/S0/F3]
  In a virtual reality (VR) environment, cyber sickness is correlated with exposure duration, with the degree of the symptoms rising proportionally as the VR session duration increases, so if possible, shorter exposure duration can help eliminate or at least minimize the onset of cyber sickness.

C2643  virtual reality exposure duration  [not defined; from fact 51/S1/F0]
  The duration of virtual reality (VR) exposure depends on the size of the virtual world, the travelling speed, the travelling time, and the interaction time spent inspecting, selecting, or manipulating virtual objects.

C2644  virtual world size  [not defined; from fact 51/S1/F0]
  The duration of virtual reality (VR) exposure depends on the size of the virtual world, the travelling speed, the travelling time, and the interaction time spent inspecting, selecting, or manipulating virtual objects.

C2645  virtual travel speed  [not defined; from fact 51/S1/F0]
  The duration of virtual reality (VR) exposure depends on the size of the virtual world, the travelling speed, the travelling time, and the interaction time spent inspecting, selecting, or manipulating virtual objects.

C2646  travel time  [defined; from fact 51/S4/F0]
  The first stage of the travel-time algorithm is to compute the time to travel between two directly connected nodes using the natural walking-speed model.

C2647  interaction time  [not defined; from fact 51/S1/F0]
  The duration of virtual reality (VR) exposure depends on the size of the virtual world, the travelling speed, the travelling time, and the interaction time spent inspecting, selecting, or manipulating virtual objects.

C2648  virtual terrain  [not defined; from fact 51/S1/F5]
  Manipulating the virtual terrain or adjusting the distances between points of interest (POIs) can reduce travel time and therefore exposure time, but arbitrary terrain changes prevent users from perceiving the true size and feel of the real space and can hamper their mental map and wayfinding in the virtual world.

C2649  distance between points of interest  [not defined; from fact 51/S1/F5]
  Manipulating the virtual terrain or adjusting the distances between points of interest (POIs) can reduce travel time and therefore exposure time, but arbitrary terrain changes prevent users from perceiving the true size and feel of the real space and can hamper their mental map and wayfinding in the virtual world.

C2650  system-controlled virtual reality tool  [not defined; from fact 51/S1/F6]
  In a purely system-automated or system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tool, users do not interact with virtual objects, so the interaction time required to interact with virtual objects can be ignored.

C2651  semi-interactive tour  [defined; from fact 51/S1/F7]
  A semi-interactive tour in virtual reality (VR) is a system-controlled navigation scenario in which travel is automatic, users may interact with objects after a navigation task is complete, and interaction is limited to a small set of objects at points of interest (POIs), while users cannot interact with other objects in the virtual environment.

C2652  system-controlled navigation scenario  [not defined; from fact 51/S1/F7]
  A semi-interactive tour in virtual reality (VR) is a system-controlled navigation scenario in which travel is automatic, users may interact with objects after a navigation task is complete, and interaction is limited to a small set of objects at points of interest (POIs), while users cannot interact with other objects in the virtual environment.

C2653  semi-interactive virtual tour  [not defined; from fact 51/S2/F0]
  In a semi-interactive virtual tour, interaction time at each point of interest (POI) can be limited to an estimate in advance of the maximum time an average user needs to interact with that POI, after which the system automatically forces the user to move to another POI.

C2654  optimum path  [defined; from fact 51/S2/F1]
  In a semi-interactive virtual reality (VR) tour, the duration of exposure can be optimized, under a limit on interaction time, by finding an optimum path that either minimizes the total navigation and interaction time required to experience all points of interest (POIs) or maximizes the number of POIs experienced within a fixed time limit for navigation and interaction.

C2655  weighted graph  [not defined; from fact 51/S3/F0]
  The virtual world part of a virtual experience is represented as a weighted graph G = (V, E), where V is the vertex set of all points of interest (POIs) and E is the set of weighted edges between POIs, representing a top view of the virtual world.

C2656  vertex set  [defined; from fact 51/S3/F0]
  The virtual world part of a virtual experience is represented as a weighted graph G = (V, E), where V is the vertex set of all points of interest (POIs) and E is the set of weighted edges between POIs, representing a top view of the virtual world.

C2657  weighted edge  [not defined; from fact 51/S3/F0]

C2658  vertex  [not defined; from fact 51/S3/F2]
  For every pair of vertices v1 and v2 in the vertex set V, the assigned edge weight is the Euclidean distance between v1 and v2 if they are directly connected, and a very large number represented by the infinity symbol if they are not directly connected.

C2659  edge weight  [defined; from fact 51/S3/F2]
  For every pair of vertices v1 and v2 in the vertex set V, the assigned edge weight is the Euclidean distance between v1 and v2 if they are directly connected, and a very large number represented by the infinity symbol if they are not directly connected.

C2660  euclidean distance  [not defined; from fact 51/S3/F2]

C2661  infinity symbol  [not defined; from fact 51/S3/F2]

C2662  optimum travel path problem  [defined; from fact 51/S3/F4]
  The optimum travel path problem covering all points of interest (POIs) is to find a path P in the given graph G that covers all vertices in V, which are the POIs, and finishes in the least possible time while maintaining a realistic speed throughout, so that the user gets a realistic feeling.

C2663  travel-time algorithm  [not defined; from fact 51/S4/F0]
  The first stage of the travel-time algorithm is to compute the time to travel between two directly connected nodes using the natural walking-speed model.

C2664  directly connected node pair  [not defined; from fact 51/S4/F0]
  The first stage of the travel-time algorithm is to compute the time to travel between two directly connected nodes using the natural walking-speed model.

C2665  actual instantaneous realistic walking speed  [not defined; from fact 51/S4/F1]
  In the natural walking-speed model, perceived instantaneous walking speed is the visual gain of 2.1 multiplied by the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act).

C2666  distance element  [not defined; from fact 51/S4/F2]
  Because speed is dx/dt, the instantaneous time dt for a distance element dx is dx divided by 2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act), and the total travel time over a distance D between directly connected nodes is the integral from 0 to D of dx/(2.1 V act).

C2667  instantaneous time  [not defined; from fact 51/S4/F2]
  Because speed is dx/dt, the instantaneous time dt for a distance element dx is dx divided by 2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act), and the total travel time over a distance D between directly connected nodes is the integral from 0 to D of dx/(2.1 V act).

C2668  integral  [not defined; from fact 51/S4/F2]
  Because speed is dx/dt, the instantaneous time dt for a distance element dx is dx divided by 2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act), and the total travel time over a distance D between directly connected nodes is the integral from 0 to D of dx/(2.1 V act).

C2669  fourier-series expansion  [not defined; from fact 51/S4/F4]
  After solving the integral with simplifications, rearrangements, and Fourier-series expansion up to n0, the travel-time estimate tau D for a directly connected vertex pair under the natural walking model is D/V naught times (3 - (16/pi^2) * sum_{k=1}^{n0} 1/(2k-1)^2).

C2670  travel-time estimate  [defined; from fact 51/S4/F4]
  After solving the integral with simplifications, rearrangements, and Fourier-series expansion up to n0, the travel-time estimate tau D for a directly connected vertex pair under the natural walking model is D/V naught times (3 - (16/pi^2) * sum_{k=1}^{n0} 1/(2k-1)^2).

C2671  V naught  [defined; from fact 51/S4/F4]
  After solving the integral with simplifications, rearrangements, and Fourier-series expansion up to n0, the travel-time estimate tau D for a directly connected vertex pair under the natural walking model is D/V naught times (3 - (16/pi^2) * sum_{k=1}^{n0} 1/(2k-1)^2).

C2672  graph  [defined; from fact 51/S6/F0]
  The algorithm takes the original graph G, with vertex set V and edge set epsilon, as input and produces the optimal time T and the path P of the minimum-time path that covers all vertices in G.

C2673  total travel time  [defined; from fact 51/S5/F0]
  For a path P in a graph that contains n vertices, the total travel time for P is the sum over i = 1 to n - 1 of the edge weight epsilon(v_i, v_{i+1}) between consecutive vertices, and epsilon(v_i, v_{i+1}) is the Euclidean distance between that pair of vertices.

C2674  travel-time minimisation problem  [defined; from fact 51/S5/F1]
  In the travel-time minimisation problem for a graph, the objective is to find a path P that contains all vertices of the graph with the minimum total travel time, and this problem is a variation of the travelling salesman problem (TSP).

C2675  travelling salesman problem  [defined; from fact 51/S5/F1]
  In the travel-time minimisation problem for a graph, the objective is to find a path P that contains all vertices of the graph with the minimum total travel time, and this problem is a variation of the travelling salesman problem (TSP).

C2676  complete graph  [defined; from fact 51/S6/F1]
  The algorithm first converts the original graph G into a complete graph G' by keeping every directly connected edge unchanged and, for each pair of vertices that is not directly connected, adding a hypothetical edge whose length is the shortest path between those vertices in G.

C2677  shortest path  [defined; from fact 51/S5/F2]
  The travelling salesman problem (TSP) asks, given a complete graph, for the shortest possible path that visits each node exactly once and returns to the starting node, where the shortest path is defined by the total weight of the edges in the path.

C2678  hamiltonian path  [defined; from fact 51/S5/F3]
  The graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem is not assumed to be a complete graph, so there may be no Hamiltonian path in that graph, where a Hamiltonian path is a path that covers all nodes and visits each node exactly once.

C2679  hypothetical edge  [defined; from fact 51/S5/F4]
  For any two vertices in the graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem that are not directly connected, a hypothetical edge is introduced for computation, and the modified edge weight epsilon dash(v1, v2) is d(v1, v2), the Euclidean distance, if v1 and v2 are directly connected, or the shortest path length between v1 and v2 if they are not directly connected, where that shortest path length is the sum of the edge weights in the shortest path.

C2680  modified edge weight  [defined; from fact 51/S5/F4]
  For any two vertices in the graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem that are not directly connected, a hypothetical edge is introduced for computation, and the modified edge weight epsilon dash(v1, v2) is d(v1, v2), the Euclidean distance, if v1 and v2 are directly connected, or the shortest path length between v1 and v2 if they are not directly connected, where that shortest path length is the sum of the edge weights in the shortest path.

C2681  shortest path length  [defined; from fact 51/S5/F4]
  For any two vertices in the graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem that are not directly connected, a hypothetical edge is introduced for computation, and the modified edge weight epsilon dash(v1, v2) is d(v1, v2), the Euclidean distance, if v1 and v2 are directly connected, or the shortest path length between v1 and v2 if they are not directly connected, where that shortest path length is the sum of the edge weights in the shortest path.

C2682  connected  [not defined; from fact 51/S5/F5]
  The shortest path lengths used for the hypothetical edges are well-defined because the graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem is connected.

C2686  complete time-weighted graph  [defined; from fact 51/S6/F2]

C2687  travelling salesman problem solver  [defined; from fact 51/S7/F4]

C2706  total importance  [defined; from fact 52/S1/F3]

C2707  virtual reality path optimization model  [defined; from fact 52/S2/F0]

C2708  waiting time  [defined; from fact 52/S2/F0]

C2709  waiting time function  [defined; from fact 52/S2/F1]
  In the virtual reality path optimization formulation, the waiting time at a node, which is a point of interest, is the maximum time a user requires to inspect or interact with the object at that node, and it is represented by a waiting-time function W that maps each node v in V to a positive real number.

C2710  total waiting time  [defined; from fact 52/S2/F2]
  For a path P with vertices v1 to vn, the total waiting time W(P) is the sum of the individual waiting times W(v_i) for i = 1 to n.

C2711  total completion time  [not defined; from fact 52/S2/F3]
  The revised virtual reality path optimization problem maximizes the total importance F(P) of a path P subject to the constraint that the path's total completion time, T(P) + W(P), is less than or equal to the time threshold T_H.

C2712  vehicle routing problem with profit  [defined; from fact 52/S3/F0]
  Vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem (VRP), an operations research problem, in which not all nodes must be visited and the route maximizes profit within a time constraint, and in this formulation profit is the importance of the nodes.

C2713  vehicle routing problem  [not defined; from fact 52/S3/F0]

C2776  precision  [not defined; from fact 54/S3/F2]
  Vector scan devices require high precision to target and excite specific pixels, which makes vector scan devices costly and typically unaffordable for mass production or mass consumption; vector scan devices are therefore typically used in specialized settings where limited quantities are required.

C2777  raster scan device  [defined; from fact 54/S3/F0]
  Graphic devices are broadly of two types, determined by the method used for excitation of pixels: vector scan devices and raster scan devices.

C2778  pixel grid  [defined; from fact 58/S1/F1]
  A display device uses a pixel grid to render an image, and points on that pixel grid can only have integer coordinates.

C2779  scanning  [defined; from fact 54/S3/F3]
  A raster scan device views an image as represented by the whole pixel grid, activates all pixels in sequence, typically left to right and top to bottom, with appropriate inputs that make the pixels emit light at appropriate intensities, and the sequential activation of all pixels is called scanning or raster scanning.

C2780  raster scan rendering  [defined; from fact 54/S4/F3]
  In raster scan rendering, pixels are excited in a left-to-right, top-to-bottom order, so the top-left pixel is excited much earlier than the bottom-right pixel; because the emitted light decays, pixels may fade out of sync and the displayed image may appear non-uniform or distorted.

C2781  vector scan rendering  [not defined; from fact 54/S3/F4]
  Raster scan rendering requires less precision and is much cheaper than vector scan rendering.

C2782  television  [not defined; from fact 54/S3/F5]

C2783  raster scan system  [defined; from fact 54/S4/F0]

C2784  frame buffer  [defined; from fact 54/S4/F0]

C2788  light-emitting element  [defined; from fact 54/S4/F2]

C2789  screen refreshing  [defined; from fact 54/S4/F4]

C2790  refresh rate  [defined; from fact 54/S4/F5]

C2791  virtual reality screen  [not defined; from fact 54/S4/F6]

C2802  display mechanism  [not defined; from fact 55/S1/F0]

C2803  local coordinate system  [defined; from fact 55/S1/F2]

C2806  device coordinate system  [defined; from fact 55/S1/F5]

C2807  viewing pipeline  [defined; from fact 55/S1/F1]

C2808  viewing transformation  [defined; from fact 55/S1/F6]

C2809  hidden surface removal  [defined; from fact 57/S4/F1]
  Hidden surface removal identifies and removes objects, surfaces, or surface points inside the view volume that are not visible from a particular viewer position because they are occluded, before the scene is rendered, to reduce computational complexity and support realistic image generation.

C2810  projection transformation  [defined; from fact 55/S1/F6]
  The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is a viewing pipeline that comprises viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.

C2811  window-to-viewport transformation  [defined; from fact 55/S1/F6]
  The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is a viewing pipeline that comprises viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.

C2812  three-dimensional view coordinate system  [not defined; from fact 55/S1/F7]
  Within the viewing pipeline, viewing transformation maps the scene from the world coordinate system to the view coordinate system, clipping and hidden surface removal operate in the view coordinate system, projection transformation maps the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation maps the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; together, these sub-stages transform a scene from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

C2813  two-dimensional view coordinate system  [not defined; from fact 55/S1/F7]
  Within the viewing pipeline, viewing transformation maps the scene from the world coordinate system to the view coordinate system, clipping and hidden surface removal operate in the view coordinate system, projection transformation maps the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation maps the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; together, these sub-stages transform a scene from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

C2815  screen coordinate system  [defined; from fact 55/S1/F8]

C2816  three-dimensional object representation  [defined; from fact 55/S2/F0]
  The fundamental objective of three-dimensional (3D) object representation is to balance the requirement to represent objects of different shapes and sizes with their intricate details so that they render realistically in a synthesized environment, rather than as simplistic geometric approximations that lose realism, and the requirement to make the operations of the subsequent stages of the three-dimensional graphics pipeline efficient in space and time.

C2817  pixel intensity  [defined; from fact 56/S10/F0]
  In intensity mapping, a lighting model computes a pixel intensity that can be any value in an infinite range between 0 and 1, whereas a display supports only a finite set of intensity values, such as 256 values per pixel on an 8-bit display.

C2818  three-dimensional object representation technique  [not defined; from fact 55/S2/F2]

C2820  boundary representation  [defined; from fact 55/S2/F3]

C2821  space partitioning based representation  [defined; from fact 55/S2/F3]

C2822  mesh representation  [defined; from fact 55/S3/F5]

C2823  parametric representation  [not defined; from fact 55/S2/F3]

C2829  attribute  [not defined; from fact 55/S3/F1]

C2831  range finder  [not defined; from fact 55/S3/F2]

C2837  polygonal mesh  [defined; from fact 61/S1/F3]

C2838  triangle  [not defined; from fact 55/S3/F6]

C2839  simple convex polygon  [not defined; from fact 55/S3/F6]

C2840  pipeline  [not defined; from fact 55/S3/F8]

C2841  spline representation  [defined; from fact 55/S4/F0]

C2842  curved surface  [not defined; from fact 55/S4/F0]

C2843  simple polygon  [not defined; from fact 55/S4/F1]

C2844  polynomial equation  [not defined; from fact 55/S4/F1]
  Spline representation is typically preferred by developers or designers of scenes who want to create an artificial environment, and it is used to construct quality scenes for rendering and to represent complex surfaces with complex properties that cannot be represented by simple polygons or simple polynomial equations.

  For n light sources, the single-light-source lighting model is revised to I_P = I_ambient plus the summation from i = 1 to n of the contribution from each light source, with each contribution calculated separately and added together, and for colored light sources each contribution is computed separately for the red, green, and blue components.

C2946  colored light source  [not defined; from fact 56/S9/F3]

C2947  intensity mapping  [defined; from fact 56/S10/F0]

C2955  multiplicative factor  [defined; from fact 56/S10/F2]

C2981  view volume  [defined; from fact 57/S2/F2]
  A view volume is a three-dimensional (3D) region in the scene that defines the portion of the scene that is projected onto the view plane, so objects inside the view volume are projected and objects outside it are discarded.

C2982  perspective projection  [defined; from fact 57/S2/F4]
  Perspective projection is a projection type in which the projectors from an object in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the view plane are not parallel and converge at a center of projection, also called a point of projection; it produces realistic rendering and is used when a realistic scene is to be generated.

C2983  center of projection  [defined; from fact 57/S2/F4]
  Perspective projection is a projection type in which the projectors from an object in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the view plane are not parallel and converge at a center of projection, also called a point of projection; it produces realistic rendering and is used when a realistic scene is to be generated.

C2984  parallel projection  [defined; from fact 57/S2/F5]
  Parallel projection is a projection type in which the projectors from the object to the view plane are parallel to each other, so their center of projection or point of projection is at infinity and they never meet.

C2985  frustum  [not defined; from fact 57/S2/F6]
  For parallel projection, the view volume is a rectangular parallelepiped-shaped region, and for perspective projection, the view volume is a frustum, with one face or side of the view volume serving as the clipping window on which objects inside the view volume are projected.

C2986  naive clipping method  [defined; from fact 57/S2/F7]
  The naive clipping method computes the intersection of view volume boundaries with object boundaries, and this calculation is computationally intensive for arbitrarily shaped view volumes such as frustums.

C2987  canonical view volume  [defined; from fact 57/S2/F8]
  A canonical view volume is a normalized unit cube into which any arbitrarily defined view volume for parallel or perspective projection is converted in order to simplify pipeline computations.

C2988  unit cube  [not defined; from fact 57/S2/F8]

C2989  point vector  [not defined; from fact 57/S2/F11]

C2990  parallel projection matrix  [defined; from fact 57/S2/F11]

C2995  perspective projection matrix  [defined; from fact 57/S2/F12]
  A perspective projection is computed by multiplying a point vector in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system by a perspective projection matrix that is more complex than the parallel projection matrix, in which D is the distance from the clipping window to the center of projection, which is typically assumed to be at the origin but not always; the obtained homogeneous coordinate values are then divided by the homogeneous factor w to obtain Cartesian coordinates.

C2996  viewport  [defined; from fact 57/S3/F1]
  A viewport is not defined on the view plane but in device space as a portion of the final screen where the scene will be rendered, and it is defined with respect to the screen or display origin and the screen or display dimensions.

C2997  device space  [not defined; from fact 57/S3/F1]

C2998  window point  [not defined; from fact 57/S3/F2]

C2999  viewport point  [not defined; from fact 57/S3/F2]

C3000  window-to-viewport transformation matrix  [defined; from fact 57/S3/F3]
  In the window-to-viewport transformation, the transformation matrix is a three by three matrix whose Sx is defined in terms of the viewport and window dimensions along the x-axis, whose Sy is similarly defined with respect to the viewport and window dimensions along the y-axis, and whose Tx and Ty are computed in terms of Sx and Sy and the corresponding x-axis or y-axis window and viewport dimensions.

C3001  homogeneous coordinate representation  [not defined; from fact 57/S3/F4]
  To obtain the transformed viewport point, the window point vector is multiplied by the window-to-viewport transformation matrix, and because the resulting point is in homogeneous coordinate representation, the Cartesian point is obtained by dividing the result by the homogeneous factor W.

C3002  cartesian point  [not defined; from fact 57/S3/F4]

C3003  computational complexity  [not defined; from fact 57/S4/F0]
  Clipping defines a view volume, discards objects or portions of objects outside that view volume, and is performed before projection so that projection is applied to fewer vertices and computational complexity is reduced.

C3004  viewer position  [not defined; from fact 57/S4/F1]
  Hidden surface removal identifies and removes objects, surfaces, or surface points inside the view volume that are not visible from a particular viewer position because they are occluded, before the scene is rendered, to reduce computational complexity and support realistic image generation.

C3005  occlusion  [not defined; from fact 57/S4/F1]
  Hidden surface removal identifies and removes objects, surfaces, or surface points inside the view volume that are not visible from a particular viewer position because they are occluded, before the scene is rendered, to reduce computational complexity and support realistic image generation.

C3006  geometric transformation  [defined; from fact 58/S0/F1]

C3007  view pipeline  [defined; from fact 58/S0/F2]
  In the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, after the viewing transformation, the view pipeline includes clipping in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, hidden surface removal in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, projection transformation from the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation from the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

C3008  continuous coordinate system  [defined; from fact 58/S1/F0]

C3009  mapping algorithm  [defined; from fact 58/S1/F2]

C3021  Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm  [defined; from fact 58/S2/F2]

C3022  line slope  [not defined; from fact 58/S2/F3]

C3023  line endpoint  [not defined; from fact 58/S2/F3]

C3025  x coordinate  [not defined; from fact 58/S2/F4]
  In Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm for line slopes between -1 and +1, the algorithm first computes delta x, the difference between the two endpoints' x coordinates, delta y, the difference between their y coordinates, and the decision parameter p, defined as twice delta y minus delta x; it initializes x and y to the first endpoint's x and y coordinates and adds that pixel to the output pixel set; then, in a loop until the other endpoint is reached, if p is less than 0 it increments x by 1 and resets p to the older p plus twice delta y, otherwise increments x and y by 1 and resets p to the older p plus twice delta y minus twice delta x, adding each computed coordinate to the output pixel set.
